title: Week 5: Health Information Exchange, Interoperability and Data Standards
overview: This week examines how authorized participants exchange health information across clinics, hospitals, laboratories, pharmacies, imaging services, public-health agencies, and other organizations. You will explore continuity of care, interoperability, exchange models and patterns, consent, privacy, trust, workflow, barriers, and public-health uses.
objectives: Explain health information exchange and its role in continuity of care.
Distinguish the exchange process from an organization that manages exchange.
Explain interoperability in clear, nontechnical language.
Discuss common benefits, barriers, consent questions, and public-health uses of exchange.
Explain the exchange process, its benefits, and the conditions needed for information to be useful and trusted.

concepts.name: Health information exchange
concepts.definition: The electronic sharing of health information between authorized participants.

concepts.name: Health information organization
concepts.definition: An entity that facilitates or manages health information exchange and may establish participation rules, identity processes, privacy protections, and technical services.

concepts.name: Continuity of care
concepts.definition: The availability of relevant information as a patient moves between care settings so that the next provider can understand recent diagnoses, treatments, medicines, allergies, tests, and plans.

concepts.name: Interoperability
concepts.definition: The ability of different systems to connect, exchange information, and use it in a coordinated way so that the information supports appropriate action.

concepts.name: Connectivity
concepts.definition: The ability of systems to send or receive data.

concepts.name: Summary of care
concepts.definition: A communication of essential information when a patient is referred or transferred, including current problems, medicines, allergies, procedures, laboratory information, demographic information, provider details, care goals, instructions, and required follow-up.

concepts.name: Authorized participant
concepts.definition: A person or organization permitted to participate in health information exchange for an appropriate purpose.

concepts.name: Patient identity matching
concepts.definition: The process of reliably associating exchanged information with the correct patient despite missing or inconsistent identifying information.

concepts.name: Data mapping
concepts.definition: The translation of local data into shared standards so that information can be interpreted across systems.

concepts.name: Centralized exchange
concepts.definition: An exchange model in which participant data are combined in a shared repository that participants query for available patient information.

concepts.name: Federated exchange
concepts.definition: An exchange model in which detailed data remain with the original organizations and a locator service helps identify where information exists before the requesting organization retrieves it.

concepts.name: Directed exchange
concepts.definition: An exchange pattern that sends information to a known authorized recipient, such as during a referral.

concepts.name: Query-based exchange
concepts.definition: An exchange pattern that allows an authorized user to search for information held by participating organizations.

concepts.name: Consumer-mediated exchange
concepts.definition: An exchange pattern that allows patients to obtain and transmit selected health information.

concepts.name: Opt-in consent model
concepts.definition: A consent model that requires the patient to agree before information is included or shared.

concepts.name: Opt-out consent model
concepts.definition: A consent model that includes information unless the patient chooses not to participate.

concepts.name: Privacy
concepts.definition: The protection of sensitive health information so that it is available only to authorized people for appropriate purposes.

concepts.name: Trust
concepts.definition: Confidence in the protections and governance of exchange that encourages people and organizations to participate.

concepts.name: Public-health use of exchange
concepts.definition: The use of information from multiple care settings for population patterns, prevention, quality improvement, planning, reporting, surveillance, alerts, immunization reporting, and disaster response.

concepts.name: Exchange workflow
concepts.definition: The process through which exchanged information is made available during a clinical task, located, reviewed, and incorporated into the current care process.

concepts.name: Standards and quality controls
concepts.definition: Shared structures, meanings, and checks that help turn transmitted data into usable information.

sections.title: Why health information must move
sections.body: A patient's health history is often distributed across clinics, hospitals, laboratories, pharmacies, imaging centers, and other organizations. Each setting may create a separate part of the record. When important information remains inside one system, care can become fragmented. Health information exchange helps authorized users obtain relevant information when and where it is needed. The goal is better continuity through access to information that supports the current care task, not the transfer of every available data element.

sections.title: Health information exchange and health information organizations
sections.body: Health information exchange, or HIE, is the electronic sharing of health information between authorized participants. Participants may include providers, laboratories, pharmacies, public-health agencies, and patients. Exchange may occur directly between two organizations or through a wider network. A health information organization, or HIO, is an entity that facilitates or manages exchange. It may establish participation rules, identity processes, privacy protections, and technical services. HIE names the activity, while an HIO names an organization that supports that activity. Not every exchange requires a separate HIO.

sections.title: Continuity of care and the patient journey
sections.body: Continuity of care means that relevant information remains available as a patient moves between care settings. The next provider can then understand recent diagnoses, treatments, medicines, allergies, tests, and plans. A patient may visit a clinic, receive a laboratory order, have the laboratory return a standardized result, be admitted to a hospital, and then return to the clinic after discharge. The clinic may need the hospital diagnosis, medication changes, and follow-up plan. HIE connects these episodes so authorized care teams can work from a more complete history. Exchanged information must still be reviewed in the context of the current encounter.

sections.title: The summary of care
sections.body: A summary of care communicates essential information when a patient is referred or transferred. It may include current problems, medicines, allergies, procedures, laboratory information, demographic information, provider details, care goals, instructions, and required follow-up. Before using the summary, the receiving team should confirm that it is current, complete, and clinically relevant.

sections.title: Benefits and conditions for useful exchange
sections.body: Patients may avoid repeating the same history and tests. Care teams can identify allergies, recent results, and medication changes more quickly, while transitions may become safer because the next provider has more context. Organizations and communities may benefit from coordination, reduced avoidable duplication, quality measurement, population-health planning, and faster public-health reporting. These benefits depend on accurate identity matching, meaningful consent, protection of sensitive information, usable workflows, and sustainable participation.

sections.title: Connectivity is not interoperability
sections.body: Connectivity means that systems can send or receive data. Interoperability goes further: systems must connect, exchange information, and use it in a coordinated way so that it supports appropriate action. Useful exchange requires shared structure and shared meaning, correct association with the patient, and fit with the receiving workflow. A scanned document may be exchanged but not searchable or reusable. A laboratory result may be transmitted while a local code remains unclear to the receiving system. Information may also be incomplete, delayed, duplicated, or attached to the wrong patient. Standards, quality controls, consistent coding, documentation, and careful data mapping help make exchanged information usable.

sections.title: Barriers to useful exchange
sections.body: Technical barriers include different EHR products, interfaces, data formats, technical capabilities, older systems, network availability, authentication, and system performance. Data differences can also change meaning: the same clinical concept may be represented with different words or local codes, while units, reference ranges, dates, status values, completeness, and level of detail may differ. Data mapping can translate local data into shared standards, but the mapping requires careful validation. Privacy, security, and trust are essential because participants need rules for access, authentication, auditing, confidentiality, and secure transmission.

sections.title: Consent and control
sections.body: An opt-in consent model requires the patient to agree before information is included or shared. An opt-out model includes information unless the patient chooses not to participate. Some models allow restrictions on particular data, providers, or purposes. More detailed choices may increase patient control but can be difficult to administer consistently. Consent requirements depend on applicable law, policy, organization, data type, and care context.

sections.title: Workflow, models, and patterns
sections.body: Exchange is most useful when information is available during the clinical task. Users need a clear way to locate, review, and incorporate outside information. Too many documents or poorly organized data can increase workload. In a centralized model, participant data are combined in a shared repository. In a federated model, detailed data remain with the original organizations and a locator service helps identify where information exists. Directed exchange sends information to a known authorized recipient, query-based exchange allows an authorized user to search participating organizations, and consumer-mediated exchange allows patients to obtain and transmit selected information.

sections.title: Population and public-health uses
sections.body: Information from multiple care settings can help describe health patterns in a defined population. Aggregated information can support prevention, quality improvement, and planning. Electronic reporting can help public-health authorities identify notifiable conditions and outbreaks. Exchange can also support immunization reporting, surveillance, alerts, and disaster response. These uses require standardized data, reliable quality, privacy protection, and appropriate governance.

sections.title: Key takeaway
sections.body: HIE electronically shares health information across authorized participants, while an HIO may provide the organization, rules, and services that support exchange. Interoperability means that different systems can exchange and meaningfully use information, not merely connect. HIE can improve continuity, coordination, decision-making, and public-health reporting, but technology alone is insufficient. Standards, quality, workflow, privacy, trust, patient identity matching, consent, and sustainability all influence whether exchanged information becomes useful and trusted.

activities.title: Separate the related terms
activities.prompt: Compare HIE with HIO and connectivity with interoperability.

items.label: Health information exchange
items.detail: The electronic sharing of health information between authorized participants.

items.label: Health information organization
items.detail: An entity that facilitates or manages exchange.

items.label: Connectivity
items.detail: The ability of systems to send or receive data.

items.label: Interoperability
items.detail: The ability to connect, exchange, and use information in a coordinated way so it supports appropriate action.

activities.answer: HIE is the exchange activity, whereas an HIO is an organization that supports or manages that activity. Connectivity permits sending or receiving data, whereas interoperability also requires shared structure, shared meaning, correct patient association, workflow fit, and support for appropriate action.

activities.title: Follow information through a patient journey
activities.prompt: Place the stages of the patient journey in the order presented.

items.text: A clinic identifies a problem and orders laboratory testing.
The laboratory completes the test and returns a standardized result.
The patient is admitted to a hospital that needs the clinic history and laboratory result.
After discharge, the clinic receives the hospital diagnosis, medication changes, and follow-up plan.

activities.title: Classify exchange barriers
activities.prompt: Place each issue under the barrier category it best represents.

items.feedback: Different products, interfaces, formats, and technical capabilities can interrupt exchange.

items.text: A local code has no clear meaning to the receiving system
items.feedback: Different words or local codes can change the meaning of exchanged data.

items.text: Participants are uncertain whether sensitive information is protected
items.feedback: Privacy protections and trust influence participation.

items.text: Outside information is difficult to locate during a clinical task
items.feedback: Users need a clear way to locate, review, and incorporate information during care.

items.text: Benefits are distributed across stakeholders, making funding difficult
items.feedback: Distributed benefits can make funding and long-term sustainability difficult.

activities.title: Choose an exchange pattern
activities.prompt: A clinic is referring a patient to a known authorized specialist and needs to send a summary of care. Which exchange pattern best fits this use case?
options: Directed exchange
Query-based exchange
Consumer-mediated exchange
Federated exchange
activities.debrief: Directed exchange sends information to a known authorized recipient, such as during a referral.

activities.title: Review a summary of care
activities.prompt: A receiving team obtains a summary of care during a transfer. Before using it, what should the team do?
options: Confirm that the information is current, complete, and clinically relevant.
Assume that every transmitted item is automatically appropriate.
Replace the summary with every available data element.
Use the summary without considering the current encounter.
activities.debrief: The receiving team must confirm that the summary is current, complete, and clinically relevant. Exchanged information should also be interpreted in the context of the current encounter.

activities.title: Compare exchange models
activities.prompt: Identify how centralized and federated exchange differ.

items.label: Centralized exchange
items.detail: Participant data are combined in a shared repository that participants query.

items.label: Federated exchange
items.detail: Detailed data remain with the original organizations; a locator service helps identify where information exists before retrieval.

activities.answer: Centralized exchange combines data in a shared repository, while federated exchange leaves detailed data with the original organizations and retrieves it from those organizations.

activities.title: Compare consent models
activities.prompt: Explain the difference between opt-in and opt-out consent.

items.label: Opt-in consent model
items.detail: The patient agrees before information is included or shared.

items.label: Opt-out consent model
items.detail: Information is included unless the patient chooses not to participate.

activities.answer: Opt-in requires agreement before sharing, whereas opt-out includes information unless the patient declines participation. Some models also allow restrictions on particular data, providers, or purposes.

activities.title: Use exchanged information during care
activities.prompt: Order the steps for incorporating exchanged information into a clinical workflow.

items.text: Make relevant information available during the clinical task.
Incorporate the information into the current clinical workflow.
Review the information in the context of the current patient encounter.

activities.title: Explain the central distinction
activities.prompt: In one or two sentences, explain why exchange is not automatically interoperability.
activities.answer: Information may be transmitted successfully but still be incomplete, delayed, duplicated, unsearchable, attached to the wrong patient, or lacking shared meaning. Interoperability requires systems to exchange and use information in a coordinated way that supports appropriate action.

activities.title: Identify public-health uses
activities.prompt: Classify each activity as a public-health use of exchange or not a public-health use described this week.
categories: Not a public-health use described this week

items.feedback: Electronic reporting can help public-health authorities identify notifiable conditions.
Exchange can support identification of outbreaks.
Immunization reporting is a stated use of exchange.

items.text: Sending information to a known specialist during a referral
items.answer: Not a public-health use described this week
items.feedback: This is directed exchange during care, not a public-health use.

quiz.question: What is health information exchange?
options: The electronic sharing of health information between authorized participants
The storage of all health information in one local record
The replacement of every local workflow with one central workflow
The transfer of every available data element regardless of need
quiz.rationale: HIE is the electronic sharing of health information between authorized participants. Its goal is access to relevant information that supports continuity, not indiscriminate transfer of every data element.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes HIE from an HIO?
options: HIE is the exchange activity, while an HIO is an organization that facilitates or manages exchange.
HIE is an organization, while an HIO is a consent model.
HIE refers only to laboratory results, while an HIO refers only to patient portals.
HIE and HIO are two names for exactly the same thing.
quiz.rationale: HIE describes the process of electronically sharing information. An HIO is an entity that supports or manages that process.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of HIE as a patient moves between care settings?
options: To preserve continuity by making relevant information available to the next care team
To prevent the next provider from reviewing outside information
To transfer every available data element whether or not it is relevant
To eliminate the need to interpret information in the current encounter
quiz.rationale: Continuity of care depends on relevant information remaining available as the patient moves between settings. The information must still be reviewed in the context of the current encounter.

quiz.question: Which condition is required for interoperability beyond simple connectivity?
options: Shared structure and meaning, correct patient association, workflow fit, and support for appropriate action
Only the ability to send a message
Only the use of a network connection
Only the existence of a local EHR
quiz.rationale: Connectivity only means that systems can send or receive data. Interoperability additionally requires information to be structured, understood, associated with the correct patient, usable in workflow, and capable of supporting appropriate action.

quiz.question: Why might a technically successful exchange still be unusable?
options: The information may be incomplete, delayed, duplicated, unsearchable, attached to the wrong patient, or lacking shared meaning.
Technical transmission automatically guarantees appropriate clinical use.
A transmitted document always has shared meaning.
Exchange is unusable only when no organization participates.
quiz.rationale: Transmission alone does not ensure usability. Problems with completeness, timing, duplication, searchability, patient matching, or meaning can prevent information from supporting care.

quiz.question: What should a receiving team confirm before using a summary of care?
options: That it is current, complete, and clinically relevant
That it contains every available item from every organization
That it never needs to be interpreted in the current encounter
That it replaces all communication with the transferring team
quiz.rationale: The receiving team should confirm that the summary is current, complete, and clinically relevant before using it during a transition.

quiz.question: Which statement describes an opt-in consent model?
options: The patient agrees before information is included or shared.
Information is included unless the patient declines participation.
The organization decides that consent is never relevant.
Only public-health agencies can use the information.
quiz.rationale: An opt-in model requires patient agreement before information is included or shared. An opt-out model includes information unless the patient chooses not to participate.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes federated exchange?
options: Detailed data remain with the original organizations, and a locator service helps identify where information exists.
All participant data are combined in one shared repository.
Patients alone transmit selected information to providers.
Information is always sent to one known recipient during a referral.
quiz.rationale: In a federated model, detailed information remains with the original organizations. A locator service helps identify where information exists, after which the requesting organization retrieves it.

quiz.question: Which exchange pattern is associated with sending information to a known recipient during a referral?
options: Directed exchange
Query-based exchange
Consumer-mediated exchange
Centralized exchange
quiz.rationale: Directed exchange sends information to a known authorized recipient, such as during a referral.

quiz.question: Which is a public-health use of health information exchange described this week?
options: Supporting reporting of notifiable conditions and identification of outbreaks
Replacing all patient-level clinical encounters
Preventing information from being aggregated across care settings
Removing the need for privacy protection
quiz.rationale: Exchange can support electronic reporting of notifiable conditions, identification of outbreaks, immunization reporting, surveillance, alerts, and disaster response.

warnings: Exchanged information must be reviewed in the context of the current patient encounter.
A receiving team must confirm that a summary of care is current, complete, and clinically relevant.
Too much poorly organized information can increase workload, so usability remains important.
Mapping local data to shared standards requires careful validation.
Consent requirements depend on applicable law, policy, organization, data type, and care context.
Technology alone is insufficient; standards, quality, workflow, privacy, trust, and sustainability also matter.
